data.text:
**Claim 0: Burj Khalifa foundation. Supported in a corrected form (pile length).**
- The official Burj Khalifa site says "The reinforced concrete mat is 3.7 meters thick and was constructed in four separate pours totalling 12,500 cubic meters of concrete." (https://www.burjkhalifa.ae/the-tower/structures/)
- Commercial Interior Design says the mat sits on 192 bored reinforced concrete piles (https://www.commercialinteriordesign.com/insight/updated-how-the-burj-khalifa-was-built-including-design-foundations-cladding-and-urban-myths).
- The 192 piles and the 1.5 m diameter are consistent across sources. The 43 m length appears in only one source I found, a Scribd student document (https://www.scribd.com/document/382908693/Construction-Of-Burj-Khalifa). That document also says the piles are 1.5 m in diameter and 43 m long, buried over 50 m deep.
- Other sources give different lengths. Several say the piles extend about 50 m below the raft, and a 47.5 m figure also appears (https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/foundation-deisgn-of-burj-khalifa/16447928). A third count of 194 piles appears in one Scribd document.
- These secondary sources disagree on pile length, so 43 m isn't firmly established.
- **Corrected form:** "192 bored concrete piles about 1.5 m in diameter and roughly 43 to 50 m long, under a 3.7 m thick concrete mat." I couldn't find an engineering or government source with the exact length. If you need a precise figure, say "about 50 m deep" or "more than 40 m long."

**Claim 1: Taipei 101 damper. Supported in a corrected form (wording).**
- Britannica calls it a huge steel sphere weighing 660 metric tons (728 short tons) (https://www.britannica.com/place/Taipei-101).
- The Civil Engineer says it's a 660 metric ton pendulum like tuned mass damper installed between floors 87 and 92 (https://www.thecivilengineer.org/news/taipei-101s-impressive-tuned-mass-damper).
- Atlas Obscura describes an 18-foot diameter, 660-metric-ton steel sphere suspended by eight cables (https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/tuned-mass-damper-of-taipei-101).
- The 728-ton figure (Amusing Planet) is the same mass in short tons, so it isn't a conflict.
- "About 660 tonnes" is correct. Two details need adjusting. It's a sphere suspended as a pendulum, not a "ball hung" loosely, and it sits at floors 87–92, which is high in the tower but not the top. It also counters earthquakes and typhoon winds, not only wind.
- **Corrected form:** "a roughly 660-tonne steel sphere, suspended as a pendulum between floors 87 and 92, reduces the building's sway from wind." It's fine to call it a "steel ball" if you want to keep the wording.

**Claim 2: Home Insurance Building. Supported in a corrected form (hedge "first" and "steel").**
- Britannica says it was completed 1885, demolished 1931, generally considered to be the first metal-frame building and, at 10 stories, the world's first skyscraper (https://www.britannica.com/place/Home-Insurance-Company-Building).
- Britannica also describes a metal skeleton of cast-iron columns, sheathed in masonry, and wrought-iron beams (same URL).
- Guinness World Records says it was erected in 1884-1885 (https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/first-skyscraper).
- The "first" title is contested. Architectuul notes that the Ditherington Flax Mill was an earlier fireproof-metal-framed building but was only five stories tall (https://architectuul.com/architecture/home-insurance-building). Planetizen discusses the "myth" of the first skyscraper (https://www.planetizen.com/features/137468-myth-first-skyscraper-how-clever-pr-campaign-duped-world).
- The frame was mostly iron, which fits the claim's "steel and iron" wording. The structure is described as cast-iron columns and wrought-iron beams, with steel used in some parts. Some sources say "steel frame" outright, which overstates it.
- **Corrected form:** "The 10-story Home Insurance Building in Chicago (completed 1885) is often called the first skyscraper because of its iron-and-steel skeleton frame, though the title is debated." Note that it was 10 stories as built, and Planetizen says nine.
